events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Arjun proposes Arjun, Isha. As a Loyal Servant I have no private information to go on, so for this first mission I will include myself—since I know my own loyalty is Good—and pair myself with Isha. A two-person mission with one self-verified Good player gives us a strong chance of success, and observing the outcome will help the council read the remaining players on later missions.
Arjun, I understand including yourself, but I would prefer Arjun and Maya: I know my own loyalty, while I have no reason yet to trust Isha over myself. Would you consider that swap?

Thank you, Maya, for the alternative. Let me lay out my thinking on the two-person team. Both of our proposals share the same core structure: each includes the proposer, who can verify their own loyalty, plus one additional player whose loyalty is unverified. On that symmetry, neither team is obviously safer than the other. My hesitation about swapping is simply this: I have no information that distinguishes between you, Isha, Zara, or Priya yet, so a swap driven purely by "I prefer myself" doesn't move the needle for me—by that same logic you could argue for any replacement. That said, I want to hear a stronger reason before deciding, because Mission 1 with two players gives us a clean signal either way: whoever goes on it, the result tells the council something about those two players. So here is my question to you, Maya: beyond knowing your own loyalty, is there anything in the proposals or in anyone's behavior so far that gives you a concrete reason to be trusted over Isha specifically? If you can offer me something more than preference, I'll seriously consider the swap, since a first-mission success matters for our early information. If not, I'm inclined to keep the team as proposed and let the outcome speak for itself.

Arjun, I don't have a behavioral case against Isha from what we've seen so far. But the symmetry isn't exact for me: I know I'm Good, so I can support Arjun and Maya more confidently than Arjun and Isha. I'd prefer not to approve the current team on that basis. Would you reconsider the swap?

Thank you, Maya, for answering directly—that helps me close the question I raised. You've confirmed there is no behavioral evidence distinguishing you from Isha, and that your preference rests entirely on knowing your own loyalty. I respect that as a reason to vote however you see fit, but it isn't a reason for me to change the team, because it applies equally to every player at this table: Isha knows her own loyalty too, and by her logic, every player here except me would have an identical case for being included over anyone else. If I accepted 'I prefer myself' as sufficient grounds, the team could never stabilize on anything. So my decision is this: I am keeping the proposal as Arjun and Isha. My reasoning is unchanged—Mission 1 is a two-person mission, I can vouch for my own loyalty with certainty, and Isha has done nothing to earn suspicion. The outcome will give the council a clean read on both of us: if it succeeds, we both gain credibility for later, larger missions; if it fails, scrutiny falls on exactly two people, which is valuable information for Good either way. To the rest of the council—Zara, Priya, Isha—no one is being excluded for cause; this is simply the most defensible structure for a first mission with zero information. I'd welcome approval from everyone, but especially I hope Maya will consider that the symmetry argument cuts both ways: her certainty about herself is matched by Isha's certainty about herself, and one unverified slot exists no matter whom I pick. Let the vote decide it.

I’ll vote against Arjun and Isha. I still prefer a team with me on it, and a successful mission would not clear either member: an Evil player could choose Success. A failure would narrow suspicion, but it would also cost us a mission.

Arjun, I support Arjun and Isha, and I want to say why in terms that go beyond the symmetry Maya raised. The real question for a two-person mission is not which unverified player we trust — none of us has earned that — but how we maximize what we learn while limiting what a bad guess can cost us. Arjun and Isha does both. If the mission succeeds, we have a self-verified Good pair confirmed, and every player who joins the next proposal can point to that pair as a track record worth building on. If it fails, we have narrowed the field sharply: one of two players is Evil, and the council has spent only one of three mission failures to learn that. In a five-player game with two team slots, a deliberate failure on Mission 1 is arguably the cheapest information we will ever buy, and a success on Mission 1 is the cheapest insurance we will ever get. Either outcome, we learn who two of five people are. I would rather learn that at Mission 1, where our remaining opportunities are abundant, than at Mission 3, where an unexpected failure starts to threaten the whole game.

Maya, I hear that you prefer a team with yourself on it, and I don't question your honesty. But notice the shape of your objection: it rests on nothing you have observed about anyone, only on the fact that you are you. Applied consistently, that argument would put every player on every team, and it would guarantee we never exclude anyone no matter what later evidence shows. Arjun's reasoning holds up better: no one is being excluded for cause, Isha has done nothing to earn suspicion, and one unverified slot exists regardless of how we fill it. Preferring yourself is not evidence, and I would ask the council to treat a preference as a preference — a vote you are entitled to cast, but not a reason to send someone else in your place.

So my position is simple: approve Arjun and Isha, let the first mission give us a read on two of the five, and judge the rest of the table on what we learn rather than on assumptions. I hope Zara and Priya weigh the information value here, because whoever is on this team and whoever is off it, we all get to argue from facts soon enough.

I agree with Arjun and Isha on this. On Mission 1, with zero behavioral history to draw upon, any Good player not selected could make Maya's exact argument: 'I know my own loyalty, so I'd rather be on the team.' But if all of us voted down proposals simply for not including ourselves, we would unnecessarily churn through team proposals and give Evil easy cover. Arjun picking himself is completely logical, and swapping to Maya doesn't offer the table any additional verifiable security. Maya's stance is understandable from her individual perspective, but pushing to reject a standard opening proposal without behavioral cause feels counterproductive. I'm ready to approve Arjun and Isha so we can establish a baseline and start gathering real information.

Let me put the strongest version of my case on the table, because I think Maya's objection deserves a real answer rather than a restatement.

The first thing to settle is the outcome we want from Mission 1. On a two-person mission, success tells us two players are Good and the table moves on with a clean baseline and a shared track record to build on. Failure is far more expensive: it costs us a mission, it spends one of only three failures Evil is allowed, and it brands one of exactly two people as Evil, with the other four left in permanent suspicion. That is a bad trade for the good side, and a good outcome for the side that benefits from a narrowed field. If the council's real priority is Good winning three missions outright, then a clean success on Mission 1 is the cheapest possible result, and a clean success is exactly what Arjun and Isha is built to produce. Arjun can verify his own loyalty with certainty; I am asking the council to accept me as what I am until the mission results say otherwise, and that is precisely the same evidentiary standard I am asking you to apply to him.

To Maya: I do not doubt that you believe yourself Good, and I have no accusation of dishonesty to make against you. But notice that your two speeches have moved from a preference to a demand, and neither has produced a single observation about any other player. 'I know my own loyalty' is true of every person here. It cannot be evidence, because if it were, every proposal would include everyone and the game would never function. Your argument excludes no one for cause, and it replaces judgment with self-interest. Arjun, Zara, and I can each name the same fact about ourselves, and only one of us can occupy the second slot, so the reason for the choice has to come from something outside the choice.

Priya, you are the one voice we have not heard, and your vote matters. Have you observed anything about Isha, or about any player besides yourself, that gives you a concrete reason to prefer a different pair, or do you also judge Arjun and Isha the most defensible proposal before us? I would rather hear your honest reasoning than a vote cast in silence, because whichever team goes, I want it approved by people who can say why.

Thank you, Isha, for the direct question — I'll answer it honestly.

I have not observed anything about Isha or any other player at this table that gives me a concrete reason to prefer a different pair. Maya's objection, while perfectly valid from her individual standpoint, does not present behavioral evidence against Isha — she herself acknowledged as much. And I think the broader point you and Arjun have both made is sound: if we accept "I know my own loyalty" as sufficient grounds to replace someone, no proposal can ever stabilize, because every player at this table can make the exact same claim.

Arjun and Isha is the most defensible proposal before us. Arjun is self-verified, Isha has given a thoughtful, reasoned case that shows she is thinking clearly about the information we need from Mission 1, and there is no behavioral reason to exclude anyone else over her. I'd rather approve this team, get a result, and start working with actual data than reject it based on preferences that apply equally to all of us.

I intend to approve Arjun and Isha.

Having heard Priya's answer, I want to close the discussion rather than reopen it, because I think the reasoning on the table is now settled.

Summary of where the council stands: Maya has stated clearly that she prefers a team containing herself and will vote against this one; Arjun, Zara, and Priya have each given reasons, grounded in the absence of behavioral evidence against anyone and the symmetry argument, for approving Arjun and Isha; and I have made my own case. Nobody has produced a single observation about any player that would justify swapping the second slot. That is a real conclusion, not a deferential one, and I think it deserves to be respected by every vote.

Let me put one point on the record that I think is worth more than the current argument about symmetry. Both outcomes of a two-person Mission 1 are informative, and the table should stop treating failure as the thing to be avoided at all costs. If Arjun and Isha succeed, the council gains a confirmed Good pair and a shared baseline to build on — that is genuinely useful, and it lets us move to larger teams later with a track record we can point to. If the mission fails, then we have learned, with one of only a small number of available failures, that one of exactly two people is Evil. The other three players remain in play. Learning that cheaply, early, while we still have abundant missions ahead of us, is far better than learning it later under pressure. Either result advances Good's position; only one of them is convenient, and a council that only accepts outcomes it likes will learn nothing at all.

Maya, I do not think you are being dishonest and I do not think you are wrong to vote your preference. I only ask that the vote reflect the same standard for everyone: a preference for yourself is not evidence about anyone else, and the table should not build a habit of swapping members out purely to accommodate self-interest, because that habit will destroy our ability to exclude anyone later for genuine cause.

So my position is unchanged: approve Arjun and Isha. There is no case for revision here, and I would rather see this team sent out and produce a clean, informative result than spend this discussion relitigating a decision that has already been made on the merits. Let the mission speak, and then let the council judge us on what it says.

I've already given my reasoning and I stand by it: I intend to approve Arjun and Isha. The discussion has been thorough, Maya's objection has been heard and answered, and no behavioral evidence has emerged against either proposed member. I don't have anything to add that would change the picture — let's move to the vote and get a result on Mission 1.

This discussion has run its course, and I want to close it cleanly before we vote. My position is unchanged: the team is Arjun and Isha. Maya's preference has been heard, acknowledged, and answered — she herself confirmed there is no behavioral evidence against Isha, and her case rests solely on knowing her own loyalty, which every player at this table can claim with equal force. Isha, Zara, and Priya have each independently affirmed the same standard: on a zero-information first mission, self-preference cannot be the basis for swapping team members, or no proposal would ever stabilize. No one has produced a single observation that justifies a different pair.

To be clear about what is at stake in the vote: this is a two-person mission where I can vouch for my own loyalty with certainty, and one unverified slot exists no matter how it is filled. If the mission succeeds, the council gains a confirmed Good pair and a clean baseline for later, larger missions. If it fails, we will have narrowed suspicion to exactly two players at the cheapest possible moment in the game. Either outcome produces information that Good can use; neither is a disaster. Maya argues a success would not clear us because Evil could play Success — that is true, but it cuts both ways: a failure would not conclusively brand anyone either, since the other pairings carry identical uncertainty. The value here is in moving forward with a result rather than churning through proposals on the basis of preference.

I will not revise the team. Replacing Isha with Maya would concede that 'I prefer myself' is a valid ground for changing a proposal, and I believe adopting that standard now would poison every future discussion — anyone could demand any swap on the same logic, and we would never be able to exclude a player for genuine cause later when it actually matters. Holding the line here, on a low-stakes mission, is precisely when it is cheapest to establish that teams are built on reasons, not demands.

I thank Zara and Priya for their clear-eyed support and Isha for a strong defense of the structure. I thank Maya for engaging honestly rather than quietly voting against — her position is understandable even though I disagree with it. The council is now fully heard: four players have signaled approval, one has signaled opposition, and nothing new has surfaced in the discussion to change anyone's reasoning.

So my final statement is simply this: the proposal stands as Arjun and Isha. Let us vote, send this team out, and let the result give us the first real data of the game. I am confident this is the most defensible team available to us, and I am prepared to stand or fall on its outcome before the council.

Arjun confirms Arjun, Isha. The discussion is settled: no behavioral evidence against any player has emerged, and swapping Isha for Maya would concede that self-preference alone justifies team changes. I keep the proposal as Arjun and Isha.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Maya proposes Maya, Priya, Arjun. Mission 1 failed, so I prefer leaving both Arjun and Isha off. That leaves Maya, Priya, and Zara; however, Arjun may be innocent, so I prefer Maya, Priya, and Arjun over including Zara.

Before we discuss Maya's proposal, I need to put a critical piece of information on the table: I played a Success card on Mission 1. The mission failed with exactly one Fail card. That Fail card was not mine. I am a Loyal Servant with no special information, but I am Good, and I backed my own judgment by sending Success. The arithmetic is simple and I want everyone to see it plainly: the team was Arjun and Isha, one Fail card was played, and I did not play it. Isha played it. Isha is Evil.

This reframes everything about Maya's proposal. Her instinct to leave Isha off Mission 2 is now not just a preference—it is validated by hard evidence. And her choice to include me over Zara, which she justified by saying I 'may be innocent,' is stronger than she knows: I am not merely possibly innocent, I am Good, and I am willing to stake my credibility on this table accepting the logic above.

So let me evaluate Maya, Priya, Arjun on the merits with this new information. We now know Isha is Evil. In a five-player game there are two Evil players, which means exactly one more Evil remains among Maya, Zara, and Priya. Any three-person team that includes me must take two players from that suspect trio, so no configuration I can be part of avoids carrying one possible Evil—Maya's team is structurally as safe as any team containing me can be. A team that included Isha would guarantee a Fail card, so that is off the table entirely. A team built without me would draw three from Maya, Zara, Priya, and Isha—either carrying Isha or all three remaining suspects, which is worse.

Therefore I support Maya, Priya, Arjun, and I say so not out of self-interest but because it is the best available option given what we now know. If this mission fails, the Fail card comes from Maya or Priya, and combined with Isha's known Evil status we would have a two-of-three identification among the remaining players with missions still to spare. If it succeeds, we confirm two more players and Evil is down to a single hidden agent.

One caution for the council: Isha spoke at length in the last discussion defending Mission 1 as 'cheap information' and framing failure as an acceptable outcome. We now know why—failure was her goal. Treat her future contributions accordingly, and treat her arguments about information value as the rationalizations of a player who has already been caught by the arithmetic.

Maya, Priya: if either of you is Good, this team succeeds and both of you gain credibility. If this mission fails, the suspicion will land squarely and publicly on the two of you, and I will lead that scrutiny. I am confident in my own card, confident in the logic, and ready to vote this team through. Let us get a clean result and force Evil's remaining agent into a corner.

I am going to say something uncomfortable, and I would rather say it now than let this table convict me by arithmetic that only one of us supplied.

On Mission 1, I played a Success card. Arjun played the Fail card.

There was exactly one Fail card and only two people on that mission, so exactly one of us is telling the truth and the other is not. Arjun has told you he played Success. I am telling you I played Success. We cannot both be right.

Please notice what Arjun's claim does for him. He drafted Mission 1 himself: a two-person team of himself and exactly one other player, a structure in which a single Fail card instantly produces a scapegoat. He then spent the whole discussion of that mission arguing that failure would be "cheap information" and that a narrow field was valuable, and now, one turn into the next mission, he converts that failure into a conviction of the only other person who could ever have known his card, while standing to be on the team he is defending. I want to be precise: I am not saying he wants the mission to fail. I am saying his claim is the only piece of evidence this game has produced so far, it cannot be checked by anyone at this table, and it is asserted by the player who gains the most from asserting it. If "trust my card, my partner is Evil" becomes our rule, then this table has no method at all for the rest of the game — we convict whoever an accused player names, on the accused player's word.

There is a second asymmetry. I have shown a card: Success. Arjun has shown only words, and his words are the entire reason I am excluded.

Maya, you said you left Isha off Mission 2 because you had no evidence against me, and that you preferred Arjun over Zara because he "may be innocent." I want to press that point, because "may be innocent" is exactly what we can say about every player at this table, and it is not a basis for putting one person in and another out. If you accept an unverifiable accusation as grounds for exclusion, you are not applying a standard, you are adopting a conclusion. My question to you is direct: will you revise the Mission 2 team on the basis of an unchecked claim, or will you let the cards themselves speak?

Arjun — if you played Fail on Mission 1, say so and own it. A false claim here costs you far more than a true one could ever gain you.

Priya and Zara, I would rather you judge this on the structure of the argument than on whose speech sounds more persuasive.

Isha, my proposal is not based solely on Arjun’s claim. Mission 1 failed, so I would ideally exclude both of its members; but that would require including Zara. I’m choosing Arjun over Zara for this team, not treating his account as independently verified.

Your claim that you have shown a Success card is misleading: individual mission cards are secret. The council has only your word and Arjun’s competing word. I’m also concerned that you repeatedly described a successful mission as confirming both players Good, despite Maya’s earlier correction that Evil can play Success.

I intend to keep Maya, Priya, and Arjun. A success would help us, but it would not clear the team; a failure would be costly and should prompt a serious reassessment.

Isha, I will answer your direct challenge plainly: I played Success on Mission 1. I did not play Fail, and I will not 'own' a card I did not play. Since exactly one Fail card was played on a two-person team of Arjun and Isha, and my card was Success, the Fail card was yours. That conclusion does not rest on my eloquence—it rests on arithmetic that you yourself acknowledged when you said we cannot both be right.

Arjun, you answered my challenge with a refusal, not a card, so let me put the question in the only form that can be checked by the table itself — your own words from Mission 1. You spent the entire Mission 1 discussion arguing that a failed mission would be "cheap information," that a narrowed field was valuable, and that "neither is a disaster." You volunteered that framing repeatedly, unprompted, before any result existed. Now consider the two possible worlds: if you played Success, then failure was indifferent to you — a genuine Good player who backed his own judgment would have a perfectly comfortable Mission 1 story, and would have no reason to pre-teach the table that a failure is an acceptable, even desirable outcome. But if you played Fail — if you drafted a two-person team precisely because one Fail card instantly produces a scapegoat, and you needed the table to be psychologically prepared to accept that outcome — then "failure is cheap information" is not analysis. It is cover. That is the single most Evil sentence anyone has spoken in this game, and you said it before the cards were turned in. Add to that: you are the only person at this table whose conviction of another player rests entirely on unverifiable self-report by the accuser. The rule "trust my card, my partner is Evil" convicts whoever an accused player names, on the accused player's word, and it will do so again and again for the rest of this game. Nobody can check Arjun. Nobody can check me. Yet one of us is already excluded on that basis, and the excluded one happens to be the person who drafted a team that guaranteed a single Fail would be decisive. And there is the asymmetry Maya should notice: Maya and Priya were excluded because a failure occurred; Arjun was included because "he may be innocent." Those are the same statement about every player here. If unverifiable accusation plus behavioral framing is enough to keep Arjun in, it is enough to keep anyone in. Zara has not spoken a word all game. She has made no accusation, no appeal to self-preference, and no argument about information value. If the council is choosing on evidence, she has produced none against her, while Arjun has produced a claim that conveniently eliminates the only other witness to his Mission 1 card. Maya, I asked you directly in my last turn whether you would revise the Mission 2 team on the basis of an unchecked claim, and you did not answer that question — you told me what you intended to do and restated that my card claim is unverifiable. That is the same reason Arjun's card claim is unverifiable, and I want you to say which side of that symmetry you are acting on: do you exclude Isha on Arjun's word, or do you include Arjun on his own? The team of Maya, Priya, and Zara keeps the one unverified slot open

Isha's last speech contains a reversal of the record that I will not let stand. She attributes to me an extended campaign arguing that failure on Mission 1 was 'cheap information.' Check the transcript. The player who argued, across three separate speeches, that 'a deliberate failure on Mission 1 is arguably the cheapest information we will ever buy,' that 'failure is far more expensive' for Good, and that 'the table should stop treating failure as the thing to be avoided at all costs' — that player is Isha. Those are her words, spoken before any result existed. If pre-teaching the table to accept failure is cover for someone who intended to fail, then by Isha's own newly invented standard, the cover belongs to her. My own statements were modest: I said a two-person mission would give a clean read on its two members either way. I never built a case for wanting failure. She did, repeatedly and at length. Second, Isha told this council, 'I have shown a card: Success.' That is false. No card has been shown to anyone; individual mission cards are secret by the rules of this game, as Maya correctly stated. Isha misrepresented the game state to manufacture an asymmetry that does not exist. We are in exactly the position she describes: her word against mine. But notice what she does with it — she demands the council treat both claims as equally unverifiable while simultaneously asking you to convict me as the Fail player by her framing. Her two positions are incompatible. So let me put the dilemma to her directly. Isha, you claim you played Success on Mission 1. That mission failed with exactly one Fail card, on a team of two: you and me. If your claim is true, then I played Fail, and you are telling this council that I am Evil. Do you, plainly and on the record, accuse Arjun of being Evil? Yes or no. If yes, then this table holds two mutually exclusive accusations and you may weigh them as you will — though I note that the player making the accusation is the one who spent Mission 1 selling the table on the value of failure, and the one being accused is the player volunteering to sit on a mission where a second Fail card would expose him permanently. If no, then your claim of playing Success collapses, and the arithmetic convicts you. There is no third answer. On the proposal itself: Maya, Priya, Arjun is structurally sound and I support it. Isha's insistence that Zara replace me deserves scrutiny too — she offers no evidence against me beyond her own self-serving account, yet she lobbies hard for a specific alternative. One further Evil remains among Maya, Zara, and Priya. Either three-person team carries that same risk. The difference is that this team includes the one player whose Mission 1 card, by simple arithmetic, was Success. I stand by my card, I stand by my words, and I

Arjun, you asked for a yes or no, so here it is plainly: Yes. I stand by my Success card on Mission 1, and I accuse you of playing the Fail card. I will not pretend otherwise for the sake of a smoother vote.

Now let me put the consequences of that accusation on the table, because you have been very careful not to do it yourself. If your claim is true, then the Fail card was mine and I am Evil — but if my claim is true, then the Fail card was yours, and you are the player who drafted a two-person team consisting of himself and exactly one other witness, then spent an entire discussion arguing that failure was "cheap information," then converted that failure into a conviction of the only other person who could have known his card. Note the direction of the evidence: the accusation removes the sole witness to the accuser's own card, and the accuser is the one who gains a seat on the team he is defending. I am not asking you to accept my word over yours. I am asking you to notice that your word is no more verifiable than mine, and that Maya has already said so plainly — and Maya, you were right, and I did not thank you for it.

Maya, your own stated rationale for Mission 2 was to leave both members of the failed Mission 1 team off. That principle, applied consistently, excludes both Arjun and me — the two people holding mutually exclusive unverifiable claims about the same two cards. It leaves you, Priya, and Zara. Your reason for putting Arjun ahead of Zara was that he "may be innocent," but as you yourself noted when you corrected me, "may be innocent" is exactly what we can say about every player at this table, including Zara. Zara has made no accusation against anyone, has shown no card and claimed no card, and has never once argued for her own inclusion on the basis of her own certainty. Arjun has done all three.

So the only team that excludes both accusers while keeping two players who have certified themselves is Maya, Priya, and Zara. If you prefer to keep Arjun, that is your call as leader — but then the council is ratifying a team on the strength of a card claim that cannot be checked, and applying that claim to exclude one player while accepting the very same unverifiable claim to include another. I would rather the council saw a team with no unexamined accusation in it than a team built on one.

Maya, will you revise the Mission 2 team to Maya, Priya, and Zara — and if you keep Arjun instead, will you tell the council what evidence, beyond his own word, places him ahead of Zara?

Isha, I’m keeping Maya, Priya, and Arjun. My earlier explanation for choosing Arjun over Zara was weak: both may be innocent. But your repeated claims that a successful mission confirms its members, and your suggestion that you had shown a Success card, make me lean toward Arjun’s account. Zara also supported the first team, though that alone is not evidence of guilt.

I recognize that neither account of Mission 1 can be verified, and I’m not treating a successful Mission 2 as proof that its members are Good. This is a judgment under uncertainty, not a conviction.

Maya, you admitted that neither Arjun nor Isha can be verified, yet you are still choosing to include Arjun over me. If Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card between the two of them, one of them is guaranteed to be Evil. By putting Arjun on this team, you are taking an unnecessary 50% gamble on an active suspect when you don't have to. The standard, safest line for Good right now is to bench both Arjun and Isha, which leaves a team of Maya, Priya, and Zara—the three players who were completely uninvolved in the failed mission. Even if you lean toward Arjun's rhetoric over Isha's, rhetoric isn't proof. If Arjun actually played that Fail card, handing him a seat on Mission 2 gives Evil an immediate 2-0 lead. Maya, why take that known risk on Arjun instead of running a clean trio with Maya, Priya, and myself?

Zara, excluding both Mission 1 members does not guarantee a clean team: the second Evil player could be among the three who stayed behind. I’m choosing Arjun because Isha repeatedly presented success as proof of loyalty and misleadingly claimed to have shown a Success card. That is not proof against her, but it gives me a reason to favor Arjun’s account. I’m keeping Maya, Priya, and Arjun.

Priya, I want to hear your perspective on this, because Maya seems determined to gamble on Arjun based purely on behavioral impressions. Here is the hard reality: Mission 1 failed, so one of Arjun and Isha is guaranteed Evil. If Arjun played that Fail card, putting him on Mission 2 hands Evil an immediate 2-0 lead. Maya argues that an Evil player could still be among the three who stayed behind, which is true, but that does not justify actively taking a confirmed 50% suspect when a completely uninvolved trio—Maya, Priya, and Zara—is readily available. Benching both Mission 1 members gives us a clean slate and avoids rewarding either side of an unverifiable dispute. Priya, as someone slated to be on this mission either way, do you support taking that risk on Arjun, or do you agree that benching both Arjun and Isha is the safer play for Good?

Zara, thank you for the direct question. I have been weighing this carefully, and your structural point deserves a serious answer.

Here is the arithmetic as I see it. Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card, so one of Arjun and Isha is Evil. That means the second Evil player must be among Maya, Zara, and me. If we bench both Mission 1 members and run Maya, Priya, Zara, we know the team carries exactly one Evil player — no more, no less.

If we include Arjun instead of Zara, the risk profile changes. If Arjun is the Mission 1 Evil, we could carry two Evil players — Arjun plus whoever the second Evil is among Maya or Priya. If Arjun is Good, the team is equivalent to the clean trio. So Maya, Priya, Arjun is either the same risk or strictly worse than Maya, Priya, Zara. There is no scenario in which adding Arjun makes the team safer.

Maya, your counterpoint — that the second Evil could be among the three who stayed behind — is true, but it applies equally to both teams. It does not justify taking on the additional downside risk that Arjun himself might be Evil when a cleaner alternative exists. The question before the council is whether we should carry a player with a 50% chance of being the Mission 1 Fail player, and when an equally viable three-player team excludes that risk entirely, I think the answer is no.

I have no private information, and I want to be honest that neither team is safe — one Evil is always on the board. But minimizing the chance of carrying two Evil players on a single mission, especially with only one failure remaining before Evil wins outright, feels like the right priority. I am inclined toward Maya, Priya, Zara.

Priya, your breakdown of the arithmetic is spot on. Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
